Move
mōōv
v. (to stir, impel, be shaken; rendering Hebrew mot, Greek phero and kineo)
From Latin moveo through French. Scripture's usage runs two directions: what God moves stands accomplished; what cannot be moved stands secure.

Biblical Definition

To move is to stir or displace — and Scripture's deepest uses are both negative and glorious. The fixed saint: “I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved” (Psa 16:8). The fixed city: God is in her midst, “she shall not be moved” (Psa 46:5). The moved prophets: “holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost” (2Pe 1:21) — borne along as a ship before wind. And the God in whom “we live, and move, and have our being” (Act 17:28) is Himself the unmoved ground of every motion.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines move as to impel, to carry or draw from one place to another, to excite into action, to affect or touch — motion of body and of heart together.

expand to see more

MOVE, v.t. To impel; to carry, convey or draw from one place to another; to cause to change place.

2. To excite into action; to affect; to agitate.

3. To touch; to awaken the feelings; to affect with compassion.

Key Scripture

Psa 16:8 — "I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved."

Psa 46:5 — "God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved: God shall help her, and that right early."

2Pe 1:21 — "For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost."

Act 17:28 — "For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring."

Modern Corruption

A spirituality that chases being moved — the feeling as the proof — and a fragility that is moved by everything: Scripture prizes the opposite pair, saints unmoved by circumstance and Scripture moved by the Spirit.

expand to see more

2 Peter 1:21 is the Reformed doctrine of inspiration in one clause: prophecy came not by the will of man, but holy men spake as they were moved — carried, as Luke uses the same word for a ship driven before the storm — by the Holy Ghost. The men were fully men, the words fully theirs, and the freight fully God's. Every theory that reduces Scripture to religious genius has swapped the mover; every reader who trembles at the word has identified Him correctly.

Meanwhile the psalmist's immovability is not stoicism but geography: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved. The believer's stability is positional — God's nearness, not the believer's nerve. A generation moved by every headline and algorithm is not more sensitive but worse anchored; the kingdom we receive cannot be moved (Heb 12:28), and its citizens borrow its steadiness.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mot (H4131), to totter or be shaken — almost always with a negative: not be moved; Greek phero (G5342), to bear or carry — the Spirit's moving of the prophets; kineo (G2795), to set in motion.

expand to see more

Hebrew mot (H4131) — to totter, shake, slip; I shall not be moved (Psa 16:8); she shall not be moved (Psa 46:5).

Greek phero (G5342) — to bear, carry, drive; moved by the Holy Ghost (2Pe 1:21), the same verb as a ship driven before the wind (Act 27:15).

Greek kineo (G2795) — to move, stir; in him we live, and move, and have our being (Act 17:28).

Usage

"“Because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved” — stability is positional, not temperamental."

"“Holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost” — carried like a ship before wind: inspiration."

"“In him we live, and move, and have our being” — every motion borrows from the Unmoved."
